title: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome. Expanding the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape
content: Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from haploinsufficiency of SHANK3, caused by 22q13 deletions encompassing SHANK3 or pathogenic SHANK3 sequence variants. While the core clinical features are well described, genotype–phenotype correlations are insufficiently understood. We analyzed clinical and genomic data from 51 pediatric patients with genetically confirmed PMS (32 girls, 19 boys; median age 8.9 years). Genetic etiologies included 22q13 deletions (n=32), ring chromosome 22 (n=4), and SHANK3 sequence variants (n=15). All patients presented with developmental delay/intellectual disability and speech disorders, 84.3% had autistic traits. Developmental regression occurred in 72.5% of the cohort and was significantly more common in patients with SHANK3 sequence variants (p=0.041). Feeding difficulties occurred more frequently in patients with SHANK3 variants (p=0.011), while lymphedema was observed exclusively in patients with 22q13 deletion. Patients with SHANK3 sequence variants were more likely to have acquired expressive language (p=0.047). The use of pointing gesture appeared to depend on type of SHANK3 variant (nominal p = 0.041). Among patients with 22q13 deletions, the presence of kidney disorders correlated positively with deletion size (p=0.012). Ophthalmological abnormalities were identified in 58.8% of patients, with refractive errors being most common. While PMS is universally characterized by abnormal neurodevelopment, the underlying genetic etiology significantly influences the development of several core and associated features. These findings underscore the importance of genetic stratification in clinical management.
